newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin visits Kremlin, opponents move to oust him.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin visits Kremlin, opponents move to oust him.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin appeared unexpectedly in his Kremlin office on Wednesday to demonstrate that he is running Russia despite a bout of pneumonia but his foes in parliament still moved to oust him on health grounds.

The presidential press office said Yeltsin, who has not been seen in public for two weeks since contracting double pneumonia, turned up at the Kremlin to discuss domestic and foreign policy with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
But there were still no pictures of the president, who left hospital on Monday after 12 days. His press office later said he spoke to Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma by telephone.
Chief Kremlin spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, dismissed a parliamentary bid to make Yeltsin stand down as legally empty.
Interfax news agency quoted him as saying Yeltsin had not reacted personally to the attacks because he was a "heavyweight fighter" and did not box "bantamweights or flyweights".
"It's not up to the president to answer every whine, to answer every sob and every criticism that come from the opposition benches," Yastrzhembsky was quoted as saying.
Yeltsin, who turns 66 on February 1, caught pneumonia just two weeks after returning to work from a half-year absence during which he had a heart bypass operation in November.
That absence has fuelled speculation about the ability of the once charismatic leader to rule Russia for the rest of the four-year second term he won in an election last July.
Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told ORT television Yeltsin would probably need two or three weeks to fully recover.
Mironov said Yeltsin's health was much better now but he also chided the Russian leader for being too hasty to show he was fit for work after getting out of hospital.

Yeltsin's communist foes in the State Duma lower house of parliament used his latest illness as grounds to restart confrontation with him and have offered a parliamentary resolution which would dismiss Yeltsin for health reasons.
The draft, initiated by Communist Viktor Ilyukhin, was put up for debate on Wednesday despite a ruling by the chamber's own legal experts who had ruled it had no legal basis.
"Either we agree to Russia's collapse or try to do something about it," Ilyukhin told reporters before the debate.
The opposition-dominated Duma approved the motion "in principle". But subsequent voting led to confusion.
Pro-Yeltsin deputy speaker Alexander Shokhin, who chaired the debate, told reporters after a second vote that the proposal to dismiss Yeltsin had been conclusively rejected.

But the chamber's press service later said that this second vote, held amid rowdy scenes, had actually been on a technical motion and its failure simply meant Ilyukhin's draft resolution itself would now be considered again by the chamber next month.

Yeltsin's personal representative in the Duma said later that the adoption of the resolution, though not constitutionally binding, could provoke turmoil in the country and prompt other branches of power to undertake counter-measures.
"If the State Duma finally approved the resolution it could provoke consequences harmful for the state, of which civil war might be the worst," Alexander Kotenkov told reporters.

"To prevent such consequences, other branches of power -- I do not elaborate on whether this could be president or judiciary -- could make decisions which would also contradict Constitution," he added, giving no details.

In October 1993, Yeltsin dissolved the Soviet-era parliament and sent in tanks to quell a rebellion by its supporters. One leading pro-government deputy said Yeltsin might dissolve the Duma but the constitution limits the president's power to do so.
As the Duma attacked Yeltsin, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov briefed the Federation Council upper house on another painful issue for Russia -- NATO's plans to expand eastward.
Primakov on Monday held talks behind closed doors with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana in Moscow.
On Wednesday, he reiterated Moscow's objections to NATO's plan, which would grant at least some of Moscow's Cold War satellites in eastern Europe full membership of the alliance.
"Russia stood and stands against the enlargement of NATO...on geopolitical, military and moral-psychological grounds," Primakov said in televised remarks.
